lesson.menu_title: The Person Who Handles the Accounts — Who Is Who
lesson.menu_desc: Relative clauses, for describing people precisely in a company of four countries -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- The Person Who Handles the Accounts
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosa M. Mitiko Shida | Lesson 10 -- The Person Who Handles the Accounts

listenings.text: Rosa, it is Beatriz. I am putting together the contact sheet for the regional office and I need three names from you before Friday. First, the person who handles pricing for your biggest accounts. Second, your backup, meaning the colleague who covers for you when you are travelling. And third, and this is the one everybody forgets, the person at the client whom you actually call when something goes wrong at eleven at night. Not the name on the contract. The real one. The sheet that we are building is going to be the thing every new colleague reads in their first week, so please give me people, not departments.

Something I tell every new account manager on their first day. The org chart is not the map of this company. It is a diagram that shows who reports to whom, and that is a much smaller piece of information than people expect. The map you actually need is different. It is the list of people who answer quickly, the people who know things that are not written anywhere, and the two or three people whose approval unblocks everything. That list is not published. You build it yourself, in about a year, and the fastest way to build it is to ask the question nobody likes asking: who is the person I should call about this?

reading.rtitle: The Map That Is Not the Org Chart
paras: Every large company gives new employees an org chart, which is a diagram that shows who reports to whom. It is accurate, it is useless, and everybody pretends otherwise for about a year.

The map that actually matters is a different list, and nobody publishes it. It contains the colleague who answers an email in twenty minutes, the analyst who knows why a system does something strange, and the two people whose approval unblocks everything. It also contains one name per client: the person you call at eleven at night, who is almost never the person whose name is on the contract.

New people build this list slowly, by asking. The question that builds it fastest is also the one people are most reluctant to ask, because it sounds like an admission: who is the person I should call about this? Nobody who has worked in a large organization for ten years has ever thought less of a colleague for asking it.

There is one more thing about the real map. It is fragile. Somebody who has been the point of contact for six years retires, and half of a department discovers that nothing about what she knew was written down. That is why a proper handover matters more than any system, and why the best account managers keep their own list up to date, on paper, for the day they hand it to somebody else.
reading.source: Column -- South America Commercial Aviation Review

items.situation: A new colleague asks who to contact about pricing for your biggest account.
tips: Who identifies a person: the colleague who handles pricing
Give the name and one detail about when to call

items.situation: You have to explain what your backup does while you are travelling.
tips: A defining clause with who, no commas
She is the person who covers for me when I am away

items.situation: You want to add extra information about a colleague you have just named.
tips: Non-defining takes commas: Ana, who joined in March, ...
The commas mean the information is extra, not identifying

items.situation: Somebody asks which route you are talking about.
tips: Use that or which for things
The route that connects Sao Paulo to Bogota

items.situation: You are describing where the regional team sits.
tips: The office where the regional team is based opened in September

items.situation: You want to identify a client by something that belongs to them.
tips: The client whose contract expires in March

extra_audio.text: Marcos explains that he is taking over two accounts from a colleague who is leaving. Rosa asks which accounts they are and who the point of contact is at each one. Marcos answers with the names and admits that one of them is only written on the contract. Rosa explains the difference between the name on the contract and the person you actually call at night. Marcos asks her to send him the list she keeps, and Rosa agrees to go through it with him before the handover.
